subject: physics
question_text: Can the velocity of an object be in a direction other than the direction of acceleration of the object? Explain.

verification.note: Unit 3 has NO Long Answer section in either source book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The Fastrack (pp.6-8) lists 4 Very Short Answer and 6 Short Answer questions plus a PROBLEMS section; the TSBIE Basic Learning Material (pp.4-5) has a Short Answer section ONLY (5 questions) and no VSAQ section. The mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Motion in a Straight Line · 4 marks

steps.label: The answer
lines: Yes. The velocity and the acceleration need
The acceleration points along the net force,
whatever the velocity happens to be doing.
steps.why: Velocity records how the body is moving now; acceleration records how that motion is being changed. They are set by different things, so they need not agree.
common_mistakes: Answering no, on the belief that acceleration must always follow the motion.

recall.must_convey: That yes, velocity and acceleration can point in different directions.

steps.memory_tip: Velocity is where it is going. Acceleration is where the force is pushing.
steps.margin_note: Say yes in the first line, then prove it.

steps.label: The example
lines: while it rises, velocity is upward,
but the acceleration g is downward.

lines.text: Here velocity and acceleration are opposite

lines: so the body slows down as it rises.
steps.why: When acceleration opposes velocity the speed falls; when it agrees the speed rises. This example is the clearest case of opposition.
common_mistakes: Using a body falling downwards, where both point the same way and prove nothing.

recall.must_convey: That for a body thrown vertically upwards the velocity is upward while the acceleration g is downward.

steps.memory_tip: Rising body: going up, being pulled down. Opposite at every instant of the rise.
steps.margin_note: Two marks here. Name both directions explicitly.

steps.label: The general point

lines.text: Acceleration changes velocity; it need not follow it

lines: In projectile motion the velocity is at an angle
while the acceleration stays vertically down.
steps.why: Projectile motion generalises the example: the two are neither parallel nor opposite, but at a changing angle throughout the flight.
common_mistakes: Claiming they must be either parallel or opposite. Any angle is possible.

recall.must_convey: That acceleration changes the velocity and need not point along it, as in projectile motion.

steps.memory_tip: In a projectile the angle between them changes all through the flight.
steps.margin_note: One general sentence closes the answer.

insider_note: Answer yes, then give one example. A body thrown upward is the cleanest — opposite directions, same instant.
